title: Matrix multiplication exponent
formal: Determine, with the absolute \(1/100\) acceptance precision below, the matrix multiplication exponent \(\omega=\inf\{\tau\in\mathbb R:\exists C>0\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge2\Rightarrow s(n)\le Cn^\tau\}\). Here s(n) is the minimum number of arithmetic gates in a circuit computing all entries of the product of two arbitrary n by n complex matrices exactly, in the model below.
definitions: For each integer \(n\ge2\), the inputs are the \(2n^2\) independent complex variables \(a_{ij},b_{ij}\), with \(1\le i,j\le n\). The required n squared outputs are the polynomials \(c_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^n a_{it}b_{tj}\). A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose source nodes are input variables or constants from \(\mathbb C\), and whose other nodes have two ordered inputs and apply addition, subtraction or multiplication. Multiple uses of a previously computed value are allowed. Each ordered output position (i,j) designates a node whose polynomial is exactly c_ij, so one circuit must be correct on every pair of complex matrices. Circuit topology and constants may depend on n, but not on the matrix entries. Size is the number of arithmetic gates, including gates operating on constants; source nodes and output designations have zero cost. No division, comparison, branching, randomness, approximation or test of the input values is permitted. This is a nonuniform algebraic model: a separate finite circuit may be chosen for each n, with no required algorithm generating the circuits or their constants. Scalar arithmetic is exact, and costs of representing complex numbers in bits are outside the model. The number of gates differs only by a constant factor from the source’s binary-circuit wire measure, and allowing an explicit subtraction gate also changes size by at most a constant factor; neither changes the exponent. Define s(n) as the least size among correct circuits. This minimum exists because the elementary multiplication formula gives a circuit, and sizes are nonnegative integers. The n squared output polynomials are distinct and none is a source polynomial, so each needs a distinct arithmetic gate and \(s(n)\ge n^2\). The elementary upper bound \(s(n)\le2n^3\) makes the exponent set nonempty and gives \(2\le\omega\le3\). The infimum need not be attained. Specifically, \(\omega\le u\) means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that \(s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{u+\varepsilon}\) for every integer n at least two. A lower bound \(\omega\ge\ell\) means that for every real \(\tau<\ell\) and C>0 there is an integer n at least two with \(s(n)>Cn^\tau\). These quantified bounds do not demand a circuit family attaining the endpoint exponent or a pointwise lower bound at that endpoint. The source’s conjecture \(\omega=2\) is one possible value of the numerical target selected for this card.
answer_criterion: Specify a real number a by an unambiguous mathematical description and give a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|a-\omega|\le1/100\) for the unrestricted circuit quantity above. Equivalently, certify bounds \(\ell\le\omega\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\) and take \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). A proved exact value also qualifies. The proof must justify both sides of the error interval, with the infimum and nonattainment conventions in the definitions. Merely copying or renaming the defining infimum, reporting an optimized upper bound, or giving a bound only for a restricted tensor method does not meet the requirement. This tolerance concerns the value of the exponent and does not assert a proof of the exact conjecture that omega equals two.
why: This exponent measures the asymptotic arithmetic cost of a fundamental operation and governs many other algebraic and graph algorithms. Determining its value would locate the limit of savings from shared computation.

importance.reason: One of the main questions in algebraic algorithms, governing a widely used primitive and many dependent complexity bounds. Both faster constructions and a superquadratic lower bound would have broad consequences.

progress.text: Strassen gives matrix multiplication in \(O(n^{\log_2 7})\) arithmetic operations, establishing a strictly subcubic exponent.
Alman’s revised universal-method paper proves that its application to any Coppersmith–Winograd tensor cannot give an exponent below 2.16805. This is a method-specific barrier.
The SODA publication of More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication states \(\omega<2.371339\).

Dupont and coauthors report \(\omega<2.371177\). Section 4 describes rational certification and says the verification repository is being prepared; that certificate has not been replayed in this review.
The third arXiv revision of More Asymmetry incorporates the later optimization while distinguishing it from the original published bound. It does not establish a matching general lower bound.

status_note: The checked source states the exponent-two conjecture, and the August 2026 papers report improved upper bounds without determining omega. The known interval displayed here remains wider than the requested numerical tolerance. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified determination at that precision. The optimization certificate was not independently replayed, and its repository was still described as in preparation in the checked version.

context_blocks.text: The usual algorithm computes \(n^{2}\) inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent \(\log _{2}7\).

The scientific target is the value of the exponent, whether it equals two or is larger. The familiar \(\omega =2\) conjecture specifies one possible answer. Because \(\omega\) is an infimum, an upper bound may approach it with a different circuit family and constant for every positive slack in the exponent. Exact scalar arithmetic over a fixed field separates this quantity from approximate numerical multiplication and hardware throughput.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

Alman proves a lower bound of 2.16805 for exponents achievable by applying the universal method to Coppersmith–Winograd tensors. That bound quantifies over a specified tensor framework. It does not imply \(\omega\ge2.16805\), because the quantity in this card permits every arithmetic circuit over the complex numbers.

An improvement in an upper bound and a determination of the exponent are different achievements. Even the reported upper bound 2.371177, together with the elementary lower bound 2, leaves an interval much wider than the required 0.02. A certified value within 0.01 would locate the optimum more closely, while still not necessarily deciding the exact conjecture \(\omega=2\).

sentences: The matrix multiplication exponent measures the least asymptotic power of n needed by exact arithmetic circuits for multiplying two complex n by n matrices.
The target permits a separate circuit for every size and counts all addition, subtraction and multiplication gates.
Its infimum may be approached without an algorithm attaining the endpoint exponent.
The accepted answer must locate the exponent with a Lean-certified absolute error of at most 0.01.
Recent upper bounds and lower bounds for restricted tensor methods do not yet give a matching interval for the unrestricted optimum.
